title: The Concession Call to an Election Winner Is No Longer a Given
summary: In a hyperpartisan era when norms and traditions cannot be counted on, some politicians are left waiting by the phone.

When the campaign trail runs out, the concession call is a tradition that is excruciating for the loser and sweet for the victor.


If it happens at all.


Last week, Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, said that his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, had never called.


“At the end of the day, it really doesn’t quite matter,” Mr. El-Sayed[told reporters](https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/politics/2026/11/07/abdul-el-sayed-mike-rogers-concede-senate-race-football-tailgate/92668112007/) . “I’m sure he had a flight to catch to Florida,” a reference to Mr. Rogers’ owning a second home near Fort Myers. (A spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers did not reply to a request for comment.)


Amy Acton, who was elected Ohio’s governor, said she had refused to take a call from Vivek Ramaswamy, her vanquished Republican rival, who in the final weeks of the campaign featured Ms. Acton’s estranged mother[calling her a liar in a TV commercial](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/vivek-ramaswamy-ad-ohio-amy-acton.html) . Mr. Ramaswamy said in his concession speech that he had called Ms. Acton and left a message congratulating her.


“I have no intention of speaking to him,” Ms. Acton told[“CBS Mornings”](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/amy-acton-vivek-ramaswamy-ohio-governor-campaign-ad/) last week. “I do believe that leaders’ words matter.”


In a bygone era, such breaches of political protocol might have been unheard of. Yet as the 2026 midterm elections wind down, with several House races and a Senate race in Alaska too close to call, one might conclude that failing to concede defeat is more frequent than ever, the latest norm of polite politics to become a casualty of a less civil age.
